items.title: Headlines for November 03, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## WSJ: U.S. Carries Out Strikes Around Strait of Hormuz on Eve of Midterm Elections Nov 03, 2026 In Iran, several explosions were reported overnight on Qeshm Island and in the port city of Bandar Lengeh, as The Wall Street Journal reported the U.S. had carried out strikes around the Strait of Hormuz. The attacks came on the eve of today’s midterm elections, which will determine the balance of power in the House and Senate, and just hours after President Trump declared that the U.S. is not at war with Iran. Trump spoke by phone with Fox News’s Sean Hannity. > President Donald Trump: “We’re not fighting a war. You know, everyone says, ’You’re at war!’ Well, when was the last time we fired anything? This isn’t a war. This is a very soft war.” The latest U.S. attacks on Iran came amid reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for a massive wave of new strikes after today’s U.S. midterm elections. That could help Netanyahu form an emergency government, following his far-right coalition’s losses in last week’s elections in Israel. This comes as Iran’s Foreign Ministry said Monday it is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the U.S. agrees to a set of demands. ## SCOTUS Rejects Trump Admin’s Attempt to Force California to Set Aside 20,000 Mail-In Ballots Nov 03, 2026 The Supreme Court has rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to force California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots it claims may have come from noncitizens. On Monday, justices issued a short, unexplained order just hours after the Justice Department filed its emergency request. An analysis by UCLA researchers found the Trump administration flagged thousands of U.S. citizens as ineligible to vote, while more than 40% of the names provided could not even be found in California’s voter rolls. In a statement, California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta said, “This latest decision should put an end to the administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders. But our work is not over. We will remain vigilant and keep fighting back against federal efforts to undermine our democracy.”

items.title: Early Edition: November 3, 2026
items.excerpt: IRAN WAR The United States yesterday attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island, U.S. officials told the Wall Street Journal. The officials said the attacks are part of a series of strikes the United States has secretly carried out against Iran in recent weeks. Earlier in the day, President Trump told Axios that he was “in no rush” to decide whether to resume fighting in Iran. Trump told other reporters that “we had a war with Iran. We won.” Alexander Ward, Lara Seligman, and Shelby Holliday report; Barak Ravid reports. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei yesterday said Iran is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the United States agrees to a set of demands. A Qatari delegation led by Ali Al Thawadi, a senior Qatari official, yesterday arrived in Iran’s capital Tehran to meet with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and continue talks aimed at achieving an agreement between Iran and the United States, sources told the New York Times. Baghaei said the possibility of opening the strait “depends entirely on Washington’s will and decision” to accept “Iran’s legitimate demands.” Erika Solomon, Sanam Mahoozi, Adam Rasgon, and Vivian Nereim report. Iran and the United States remain far from a deal to end the war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters today. The official said “mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington.” and that “Tehran’s conditions must be met if the US wants Hormuz reopened.” Parisa Hafezi reports. ... Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have advanced to within 50 miles of Aden, the temporary capital and stronghold of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, military sources told Reuters yesterday. The advance brings the Houthis closer to Aden than at any point since the early months of Yemen’s civil war in 2015, when they briefly entered the city before being driven out. Mohammed Ghobari reports. RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region Gov. Mykhailo Semikin today said at least 29 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution center in the village of Komyshuvakha yesterday, while another 10 people were injured and 48 were reported missing. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack “utterly horrific,” and said Russia “could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week.” Jaroslav Lukiv reports for BBC News. Russia’s Yaroslavl region Gov. Mikhail Yevrayev today said Ukraine set fire to a major oil refinery in ... Ukraine has struck the Slavneft Yaroslavnefteorgsintez oil refinery at least twice before. Yevrayev said air defense forces had repelled an attack on the refinery involving 124 drones and that two employees had been injured. Reuters reports. Zelenskyy yesterday warned Russia could use today’s U.S. midterm elections to launch a massive attack against Ukraine. Zelenskyy on social media said Ukraine has “intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country- primarily targeting energy and logistics,” and that the “assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine… will be overlooked.” Mira Bhakta reports for The Hill. U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff yesterday said the United States, Russia, and Ukraine will hold peace talks on Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi. U.S. officials told Axios that the meeting to restart a diplomatic effort is a result of talks Witkoff and U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner held with Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin in recent weeks. Witkoff said discussions “will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace.” Barak Ravid reports.

items.title: National and International News in Focus: Nov. 3 | Local | wktv.com
items.excerpt: ## Midterm elections are coming to a close as voters pass judgment on Trump's second term WASHINGTON (AP) — Midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s second term are coming to a close. Americans angry over high prices and an unpopular war with Iran decide on Tuesday whether to drastically shift power in Washington. Democrats are cautiously optimistic about their prospects. Democrats have watched Republicans spend the campaign’s final stretch dumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily just two years ago. Democrats are betting that discontent over Trump’s failure to deliver on his promise to tackle rising costs will depress Republican turnout and drive their own voters to the polls. ## Election Day arrives after a surge in early voting, with observers keeping close watch at the polls WASHINGTON (AP) — The first polling sites have opened across much of the East Coast on Election Day in the U.S. midterm elections, with voting unfolding largely smoothly so far. In New York's Westchester County, where some voters are casting ballots in a competitive U.S. House race, an issue with voting machines accepting paper ballots was requiring ballots to be diverted to emergency bags for later counting, but voting was ongoing. Heavy rains and flash flooding in the Southwest are expected to make it harder for some voters to reach polling places Tuesday, and officials have announced some polling location changes. The final day of voting arrives against a backdrop of uncertainty after a year in which President Donald Trump has tried to interfere in how states run their elections. ... ## US will halt $4B in aid to Israel as the Mideast ally shifts to buying military hardware, Trump says WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says the U.S. will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East. The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call Tuesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they've been talking about it for a couple of years. Trump says Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also says U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Netanyahu’s office hasn't commented. ... ## US strikes Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, official says, leaving unclear what comes next A U.S. official says the United States has launched strikes on Iranian targets. It appeared to be a limited operation on the eve of Tuesday’s crucial midterm elections. Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. Unlike earlier in the war, the strikes were not publicly announced. President Donald Trump had previously said the U.S. wouldn’t launch strikes on Iran before the midterms. A U.S. official said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait. The official wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. ## Death toll hits 31 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with dozens still missing KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — The death toll from a Russian attack in southern Ukraine has risen to 31, with dozens still missing. People had gathered to receive humanitarian aid when the attack occurred. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles overnight across nine regions. He noted the barrage coincided with U.S. elections. The attack Monday in a village in Ukraine’s southern Zaporizhzhia region targeted a school building and a nearby shelter. In Kharkiv, a combined missile and drone attack injured at least 62 people. In the Dnipro area, a Russian attack killed one person and wounded 17. Rescue efforts are ongoing.

items.title: In top Senate race states, gas, grocery and housing costs are up
items.excerpt: Nov. 3, 2026, 7:44 AM EST By Alexandra Meier From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day. In 2024, President Donald Trump’s promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him win back the White House. But nearly two years into his second term, Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran have driven costs higher across the country, fueling deep discontent among voters. These frustrations aren’t confined to voters who support Democrats. More than half of Republicans, 53%, are dissatisfied with the state of the economy, according to the latest NBC News poll. ... ## Pain at the pump In several of the states with close Senate races, voters face gas prices that have climbed higher, and more sharply, than the mean nationwide prices over the same period. Across the country, the average cost of a gallon of gas has risen 40% since Feb. 28, the day Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched attacks on Iran that sent crude oil prices through the roof. Right before the war, the average price of unleaded was $2.98 per gallon, according to NBC News’ gas price tracker. On Monday, it was $4.16. In Iowa, however, the average price has climbed by significantly more, nearly 55% since late February. The same figure applies in Nebraska. In Kansas, gas prices are up by 53%. All three states broke for Trump in 2024. ... Drivers in Michigan are also experiencing an outsized jump, with gas up 51% from $2.99 in February to $4.52 Monday. There, Democrat Abdul El Sayed is facing off against Republican Mike Rogers. In Ohio, where Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown is challenging incumbent Republican Jon Husted, the price of a gallon of gas has climbed by 48%. “We aren’t going very many places,” Kathy DiCristofaro, of Youngstown, Ohio, told NBC News. “We’re retired and have had to cancel trips,” she said. In Maine, the price of a gallon of gas is 46% higher than it was before the war, creating a drag on Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and an opportunity for Democrat Troy Jackson. Even when national average gas prices pivot lower, as they did throughout October, that doesn’t always extend to parts of the country where refinery activity influences fuel costs, particularly in the Great Lakes region. Far from the coasts, refineries that service Michigan, Ohio and Iowa cannot easily restore supply lost to weather events or refinery capacity. “When you’re isolated in the interior of the country, these problems can linger as long as the refinery is experiencing issues,” said Patrick De Haan, chief petroleum analyst at GasBuddy. ## Tariffs hit home Beyond the gas pump, voters are also feeling the sting of higher oil prices overseas in the form of increased transportation costs for groceries and retail goods. In several of the states with tight Senate races, average households are spending a lot more of their monthly income on groceries than shoppers elsewhere in the country, according to a WalletHub study. Among the 10 most cost-burdened cities for groceries in America, three of them are in Ohio: Cleveland, Toledo and Cincinnati. ... While higher diesel costs have raised the price of transporting everyday goods, many businesses have also passed another big new cost on to consumers in the past two years: tariffs. ... The lion’s share of these costs have come in the form of new import duties that affected the price of cars and trucks. But across the country, tariffs will cost every household an additional $1,100 this year, on average, according to estimates from the Yale Budget Lab. ... ## Your money buys you less While Americans are technically earning more in dollar terms on average, paychecks are not keeping up with the pace of inflation. Wages in September grew by 3.0% year over year. But the annual inflation rate hit 3.7%. Adjusting for inflation, this means average hourly earnings nationwide fell by about 0.7%. This disparity is another source of economic pressure on voters going into Election Day. But the gap between wage growth and inflation is significantly wider in some of the states that will be most closely watched Tuesday night. In Nebraska, purchasing power fell by 3.5% over the three months ending in August, relative to regional inflation. Iowa saw a drop of 2.6%. And in Alaska, real pay fell by 2.0% compared to the same period last year.

items.title: Crude oil prices fall for second day as market hopes for diplomatic resolution to Iran war
items.excerpt: Published Tue, Nov 3 2026 1:41 AM EST Updated 45 Min Ago ... Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months. U.S. West Texas Intermediate Add To Watchlist futures were 63 cents lower to $95.83 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier. Brent crude Add To Watchlist futures, the international benchmark, were down $1.59 at $103.18 a barrel. The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal. Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen." Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said. However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency. The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections, as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response. ... High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections. Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.

items.title: Treasury yields rise ahead of midterm vote and jobs data
items.excerpt: Treasury yields moved higher on Tuesday as voting began in the U.S. midterm elections, while investors parse a busy week of economic data and monitored Middle East tensions. The 10-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose more than 4 basis points to 4.935%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist — which tends to move more on geopolitical developments — was up 4 basis points at 5.309%. The 2-year Treasury note Add To Watchlist yield, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was up more than 2 basis points at 4.608%. ... On the economic front, September's JOLTS job openings report showed an increase to 7.523 million, beating out the 7.125 million that economists polled by Dow Jones were expecting. ISM services PMI and ADP employment figures are due on Wednesday, with October's nonfarm payrolls and unemployment expected Friday, in a busy week for domestic economic data.

items.title: Election Day underway after a surge in early voting, as Trump sows doubt on results | PBS News
items.excerpt: Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:48 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The final day of voting in this year's midterm elections arrived Tuesday against a backdrop of uncertainty after a year in which President Donald Trump has tried to interfere in how states run their elections and sown doubts about the outcome should Republicans lose. Millions of Americans already have cast their ballots, with early voting turnout on pace to eclipse that of the last midterm elections. In contrast to the president's continued rhetoric about election cheating, voting so far has unfolded with relatively few problems. Trump has spent months trying to use the power of the presidency to put his thumb on the scale of this year's elections, which will determine whether his party keeps control of Congress. His Justice and Homeland Security departments have been involved in a massive hunt for voters who are not U.S. citizens, at one point engaging in a made-for-the-cameras predawn operation that led to more than two dozen arrests in California. The Department of Justice was planning its largest-ever effort to monitor Election Day polling places, countered by an even larger effort among Democrats and allied groups, and at the president's urging had sued to block certification of Alaska's results if the outcome of the Senate race favored Democrats. At the same time, Trump's constant false claims about widespread voter fraud led election officials and Democratic groups across the country to plan for the possibility of immigration agents at voting sites or federal officers seizing voting machines. His administration has insisted that no armed federal officials would be guarding the polls on Election Day. ### Courts have blocked the Trump administration's efforts to influence elections In the run-up to Tuesday, none of the steps Democrats most feared had come to pass, and the Republican administration's legal maneuvers had been largely blocked by the courts. One of the Trump administration's most high-profile attempts to interfere in state elections was turned away Monday night by the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected its push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots as part of its search for noncitizen voters. In another Monday night ruling, a federal judge said the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials. Even the administration's own record of arrests and charges has demonstrated what research and state investigations have made clear for years — that instances of noncitizens casting ballots are extremely rare. Monday's rulings followed another defeat for the president at the Supreme Court less than two months ago, when it rejected his attempt to limit mail balloting through changes at the Postal Service. That directive was included in one of two executive orders Trump has signed during his second term that attempted to federalize certain aspects of elections, even though the Constitution gives the states, and sometimes Congress, the authority to set election rules. ### Voting begins smoothly with some weather disruptions in the Southwest The first polling sites were open Tuesday morning across much of the East Coast, with few disruptions so far. In New York's suburban Westchester County, where some voters are casting ballots in a competitive U.S. House race, election officials said an issue with voting machines accepting paper ballots was requiring ballots to be placed in emergency bags for later counting. But they stressed that the ballots would remain secure and monitored, that they would later be counted and that voters could continue casting ballots while they worked to resolve the issue. ... Heavy rains and flash flooding in a swath of the Southwest were expected to make it harder for some voters to reach polling places in parts of Colorado, Arizona, Utah and New Mexico. Election administrators in the Navajo Nation announced changes to several of its polling locations, and in Utah's rural San Juan County, voters were being allowed to vote electronically on Tuesday because some of them may not be able to reach polling places. Election administrators and voting rights advocates have been advising voters casting late absentee ballots to use drop boxes or deliver them to polling places in person rather than mail them. The advice came after concerns emerged that recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations could result in postmarking delays that would mean mail ballots could not be counted. Late-arriving ballots or late postmarks disenfranchised tens of thousands of voters in California, Oregon and Washington, which mail ballots to all voters, during this year's primaries. ### Trump hasn't committed to accepting the election results The most significant disruptions ahead of Election Day were the Trump administration's attempts to interfere. Voting rights groups, Democrats and the Justice Department have been exchanging a flurry of legal filings over alleged noncitizen voters, federal election monitors, federal intimidation of election officials and other concerns. They reveal how Trump's attempts to expand federal control over state-run elections — combined with high-stakes races — are resulting in court battles that could extend past Election Day into ballot counting and certification of the results. Election law experts said Trump's lawsuits go beyond historic norms, but they said the administration's legal arguments were unlikely to convince the courts. Trump also has ramped up his own equivocations about whether the election will be legitimate, as he has in the past. A week before Election Day, when a reporter asked him if he would accept the results, he offered a qualified answer. "I will if they are honest," he said.

items.excerpt: - Nov 3, 2026 ... Movie Review: In 'Godzilla Minus Zero,' human-scaled melodrama stomps out the kaiju fun Even Godzilla can be felled by an old hazard: the sophomore slump. Though Godzilla has been stomping around for more than half a century, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is a sequel. It follows the quite excellent, Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One,” a reset for the kaiju franchise that brought Godzilla back to its postwar Japan roots. Like its predecessor, the follow-up marries human-scaled drama with a flair for stompy-stomp spectacle. Yet AP Film Writer Jake Coyle says those calibrations are slightly off in “Godzilla Minus Zero.” In his review, Coyle writes that the melodrama on the ground overtakes the movie, sagging it with a bloated story that leaves you pining for the big guy to turn up again. NEW YORK (AP) — David Mendizábal is directing a revival of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s "In the Heights," a musical that was Mendizábal's introduction to theater. The show, running for three weeks at New York City Center, features a new cast of Latino artists. Mendizábal emphasizes the importance of showcasing Latino communities, especially now. Miranda, who starred in the original production, reflects on the musical's enduring relevance. The revival comes amid immigration tensions, highlighting themes of gentrification and community. New and old cast members say the musical remains a celebration of the Latino immigrant experience, with its messages resonating strongly today. NEW YORK (AP) — My Chemical Romance has hit No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with “The Black Parade (20th Anniversary Deluxe Edition).” This reissue of their 2006 rock opera includes six bonus tracks. Back then, it debuted at No. 2 due to competition from Disney’s “Hannah Montana” soundtrack. The reissue's success is driven by 20 physical variants and a significant increase in album sales. The band’s reunion and anniversary tour have also fueled interest. Nostalgic fans and new listeners are connecting with the album's unique style and themes. This marks the longest wait for an album to reach No. 1. WASHINGTON (AP) — The Kennedy Center has announced that Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell will be honored at this year's Kennedy Center Honors. The event will take place away from the iconic venue for the first time due to President Donald Trump's legal battle over renovations and naming rights. The nominees have had substantial careers in their fields. Mamet is a renowned playwright, while Mandrell is a Country Music Hall of Fame member. Anka, a longtime friend of Trump, has rewritten “My Way” with MAGA-themed lyrics. The ceremony will be held on December 7 at Washington's Capital One Arena.

items.title: Movie News: 3rd November 2026
items.excerpt: ### Wicker’s UK number one, Clayface’s quiet global win, Jailer 2 breaks ₹800 crore, Marrakech’s line-up, the AFM, Iceman casting & Carrie turns 50. M ... Yesterday I promised you the UK-Ireland chart and the Jailer 2 numbers, and they’ve both landed. Tuesday also means our weekly lap of the world’s other film industries, plus there’s a very special anniversary. UK and Ireland box office: Black Bear’s Wicker had the first number one film in its distributor’s history, opening to £1.7 million from 676 cinemas, a £2,515 average, which rises to £1.8 million including previews. A24’s Primetime, starring Robert Pattinson as To Catch a Predator‘s paedo-hunting host Chris Hansen, opened in third place with £1.3 million from 560 cinemas, a £2,321 average, and £1.7 million with previews. Clayface dropped 37% in its second weekend to £1.2 million, taking it to £4.7 million. It’s a Halloween weekend for the re-releases, too, with Pan’s Labyrinth in 384 cinemas, Donnie Darko in 202 and Ken Russell’s The Devils in 73 in a new 4K restoration from BFI Distribution. The weekend box office, worldwide: Clayface topped the worldwide chart for a second weekend with an estimated $22.8 million, which is dismally low for a chart-topping film, as a lack of significant new releases over Halloween weekend left the market becalmed. The UK and Ireland is its biggest international market, with $6.1 million to date. Laika’s astounding Wildwood moved up to second place after international expansion, and Wicker was seventh with a $7 million start, made up of $4.1 million from North America and $2.6 million from nine international markets. In the UK, Wicker‘s opening beat those of Poor Things and The Shape of Water, according to Deadline. Elsewhere, Resident Evil has now passed $400 million worldwide. In North America, yesterday’s estimates have been confirmed, and You Can See Everything came out on top with $11.4 million in its third weekend, a little higher than expected, ahead of Clayface with $11 million. Clayface now has $44.6 million in North America and $83 million worldwide, while the whole weekend came in at roughly $60 million, one of the slowest of the year. Tamil cinema: Jailer 2 breaks ₹800 crore: Rajinikanth’s Jailer 2 passed ₹800 crore worldwide on its 18th day, finishing its third weekend with a worldwide gross of ₹807.25 crore (about $84 million), according to Sacnilk. It’s the first Tamil film to pass both ₹700 crore and ₹800 crore, and it now stands as the highest-grossing Tamil film ever and reportedly the second-highest-grossing Indian film of 2026. It has earned ₹456.3 crore net in India (about $48 million) and ₹273.5 crore (about $28 million) overseas, and it added ₹26.4 crore net in India over its third weekend. The Far East: Resident Evil’s China hold: In mainland China, Resident Evil was number one for a fourth consecutive weekend with RMB 28.5 million ($4.3 million), taking it to $71.3 million since its 5 October opening. The crime drama Traces of Justice remains ahead overall with $98.5 million since 1 October. The wider market had a quiet weekend with $18.2 million, and the year-to-date total of $4.73 billion is down 29.0% on 2025. A 2014 re-release of John Wick opened in third place. Marrakech’s line-up: The 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, which runs from 20 to 28 November, has unveiled a line-up of 76 films from 39 countries, including 10 world premieres. As I mentioned when it closed the London Film Festival, Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut opens the festival, and Marion Cotillard presides over the competition jury. Gala screenings include Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial and James Gray’s Paper Tiger, and 14 films compete for the Étoile d’Or, including Yoon Dan-bi’s The World Before and Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Ben’imana. The American Film Market gets going: Hockey’s Hollywood moment, largely driven by the success of Heated Rivalry, has reached the AFM, with Liam Neeson set to play a legendary coach in Believe 13, about his bond with an injured high school star. Closer to home, Guy Pearce, Sabrina Impacciatore, Rachael Stirling and Selena Tan have joined Jeff Daniels in Trudie Styler’s The Reception, a chaotic wedding-party comedy that’s currently shooting on location in Scotland. Iceman casting: Ben Wang, the star of Karate Kid: Legends, who also plays District 12 tribute Wyatt Callow in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping on 20 November, is in talks to play Iceman in Marvel’s X-Men reboot, which Jake Schreier is directing for 2028. The deal isn’t done, and Gabriel LaBelle, Jackson Kelly and Rhenzy Feliz all reportedly tested for the part. It would leave Beast as the only member of the original team without an actor, and the casting news arrives just days after Patrick Stewart’s farewell as Professor X was confirmed.
